research.approach: Practitioners finish the close first so actuals are reconciled and accrual-based, then put budget and actuals side by side at the same level of detail. They compute dollar and percentage variance with one sign convention, for the month and year to date, and flag only lines that cross both a percentage and a dollar threshold agreed in advance. Each flagged line gets a written cause labelled timing, price, volume or plan error, and permanent changes are fed back into the forecast. The report puts a short summary on top, the table beneath and brief commentary on the few lines that matter, and runs on a fixed monthly schedule.

steps.name: Map the chart of accounts to the budget categories
steps.why: Budget and actuals must be compared at the same level of detail, or the variances are mapping noise.

steps.name: Use closed, reconciled, accrual-based actuals
steps.why: A report built on unreconciled actuals is worse than none, and payroll must tie to the ledger.

steps.name: Compute variance in dollars and percent, for the month and year to date
steps.why: One sign convention and both measures show size and relative importance.

steps.name: Flag only lines that cross a dual threshold agreed in advance
steps.why: A percentage and a dollar floor keep trivial lines out and keep the review short enough to happen monthly.

steps.name: Explain the biggest variances with a labelled cause
steps.why: A variance is a symptom; the cause (timing, price, volume or plan error) decides the action.

steps.name: Lay out the report on one page
steps.why: Summary on top, table beneath and a few lines of commentary make a ten-minute read.

steps.name: Run it on a fixed monthly schedule and reforecast permanent changes
steps.why: A routine keeps the report alive, and recurring variances call for a changed forecast, not the same explanation every month.

pitfalls.text: Comparing budget and actuals at different levels of detail, or using bank balances and miscategorised transactions as actuals.
Recording what happened without explaining why, or treating every variance as a problem.
Explaining the same recurring variance every month instead of reforecasting the line.
Ignoring favourable variances, which hide lessons and plan errors.
Setting the commentary rules only during the review, so people argue about them mid-meeting.

hypotheses.statement: Xero accounts and budget categories do not line up, so some variances are mapping noise.
hypotheses.test: Map each account to a budget category and list unmapped accounts, budget lines without accounts and lines mapped many-to-one.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Active accounts or budget lines are unmapped, or total actuals by category differ from the Xero profit and loss.
hypotheses.refute_if: Every active account maps cleanly and totals tie.

hypotheses.statement: Payroll is the largest cost and drives at least one of the top variances, and it may not tie between Gusto and Xero.
hypotheses.test: Compare Gusto totals with Xero payroll expense by month, and payroll share of the top three variances.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Payroll is among the top three variances or the two sources disagree.
hypotheses.refute_if: Payroll ties and is small against the other variances.

hypotheses.statement: The January budget rested on assumptions that proved wrong, so the same variances repeat in the same direction.
hypotheses.test: Check whether variances on the same lines have the same sign in three or more months.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Several lines miss in the same direction month after month.
hypotheses.refute_if: Variances change sign or are one-off.

hypotheses.statement: Some variances are timing (annual fees, project billing, missing accruals) and reverse within the year.
hypotheses.test: Compare the month and year-to-date variance and look for annual or lumpy transactions behind the top lines.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A big month variance shrinks in year to date or traces to a single lumpy item.
hypotheses.refute_if: Year-to-date variance is as large as the month.

hypotheses.statement: Uncategorised or catch-all lines hide real spending.
hypotheses.test: List uncategorised, suspense and 'other' accounts and their amounts by month.
hypotheses.confirm_if: They hold a material share of costs.

hypotheses.statement: The biggest gap is revenue (project timing or client mix) rather than cost overspend.
hypotheses.test: Rank revenue and cost variances together by dollars and read the revenue lines by month.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A revenue line is in the top three variances.
hypotheses.refute_if: Cost lines make up the top three.
